items.body:
# Sources and authority

## Why the kind of source matters

Suppose a friend tells you, "Latter-day Saints believe that God lives near a star called Kolob." Another friend says, "Latter-day Saints believe that Jesus Christ is the Savior of the world." Both sentences begin the same way, and both can be traced to something written by Latter-day Saints. Yet they are not the same kind of claim. The second names the center of the faith. The first draws on a short passage in the Book of Abraham (Abraham 3) whose meaning Church members discuss in different ways, and which is not a focus of the Church's teaching today.

Most confusion about Latter-day Saint doctrine, from members and observers alike, starts here. A sentence is quoted, the quote is real, and the conclusion drawn from it is much larger than the source can carry. The remedy is not suspicion of every source. It is learning to ask, every time, what kind of source this is and what it can actually show.

This module gives you four categories to work with: canonical scripture, institutional teaching, commentary, and historical records. They are not a ladder where the top rung wins every argument. They are different tools that answer different questions. By the end of the module you should be able to place a source in its category, say what it can and cannot establish, and record it in a way that keeps your later claims honest.

A word about what this course measures. You will be assessed on whether you can describe Latter-day Saint teaching accurately and use sources carefully. You will never be asked whether you believe it. A careful explanation is a skill, and it is the same skill whether you are a lifelong member, a curious neighbor, or a scholar of religion.

## The standard works: an open canon

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints recognizes four books of scripture, called the standard works: the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price. Together they form the canon, the collection the Church accepts as scripture for the whole body of members. When a lesson in this course says a teaching is "canonical," it means the teaching appears in one of these four books.

Each book has its own character. The Bible is shared with other Christians, and Latter-day Saints in English have long used the King James Version. The Book of Mormon presents itself as a record of ancient peoples in the Americas and of Christ's ministry among them. The Doctrine and Covenants gathers revelations and inspired documents, most of them from Joseph Smith's lifetime. The Pearl of Great Price is the smallest. It contains the Book of Moses, the Book of Abraham, Joseph Smith—Matthew, Joseph Smith—History, and the thirteen Articles of Faith you will read in this module.

Two of those articles describe how the canon itself is understood. Article of Faith 8 accepts the Bible "as far as it is translated correctly," and the Book of Mormon as the word of God. Article of Faith 9 reaches forward: the Church believes "all that God has revealed, all that He does now reveal," and that God "will yet reveal many great and important things." This is what an open canon means. The collection is not assumed to be finished.

The canon has in fact grown in living memory. In 1976 two revelations were accepted into scripture by the vote of a general conference, and in 1981 they became sections 137 and 138 of the Doctrine and Covenants. In 1978 the announcement known as Official Declaration 2 was presented to a general conference and accepted the same way. Additions to the canon are rare, formal, and presented to the membership. That is part of what makes the standard works a stable starting point. When you cite a passage from them, anyone can check it, and its status is not in dispute.

Canonical does not mean self-interpreting, though. A verse can be quoted accurately and still be stretched. The Kolob example above is canonical text, but the claim built on it is an interpretation. Keeping those two apart, the words of the passage and the reading you give it, is the first habit of careful study.

## Institutional teaching: how the Church speaks today

Scripture is not the only way the Church teaches. Members are taught each week from Church-published manuals, and twice a year, in April and October, general conference brings addresses from Church leaders that are published afterward. The Church's website hosts Gospel Topics pages and essays that explain teachings and history. There are formal documents too, such as "The Family: A Proclamation to the World," issued in 1995.

Who decides what the Church teaches? The Church's own guide, "Approaching Latter-day Saint Doctrine," published by its newsroom in 2007, gives a direct answer. Doctrine is established by the First Presidency and the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles, who counsel together, and it is consistently proclaimed in official Church publications. The guide names where doctrine is found: the four standard works, official declarations and proclamations, and the Articles of Faith.

The guide also says something that surprises many readers. Not every statement made by a Church leader, past or present, is doctrine. A single statement by one leader on a single occasion often represents a personal, though considered, opinion. It is not meant to be binding on the whole Church. The guide warns that isolated statements are often taken out of context and given a weight they were never meant to carry.

How does that fit with scripture? Doctrine and Covenants 68 is often quoted here. Its first verses were addressed to Orson Hyde and offered as an "ensample" to others ordained to the priesthood. Verse 4 says that "whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture." Latter-day Saints read this as a description of inspired teaching. Notice what the verse does and does not say. It ties scripture in this broad sense to the influence of the Holy Ghost. It does not say every sermon is canon, and it says nothing about adding words to the standard works. The guide and the verse together point the same way: authority comes from inspiration and from the councils that establish doctrine, not from a speaker's title alone.

So institutional teaching is a category of its own. A current Gospel Topics page or an address published by the Church shows how the Church teaches and explains something today. That is valuable evidence. It is not the same as canon, and an older statement by one leader is not the same as either.

## Commentary: useful, but someone's reading

A great deal of what people read about Latter-day Saint belief is commentary: books, podcasts, articles, classes and websites in which an author explains, defends, criticizes or applies the faith. Some commentary is excellent. Some is published by authors who held high Church office. Some of it is the most helpful reading you will find on a topic.

Commentary's defining feature is that it is one person's reading. An author may quote scripture or institutional sources accurately, but the argument the author builds from them belongs to the author. Quoting an Article of Faith does not turn a devotional book into scripture, any more than quoting the Constitution turns a newspaper column into law.

Consider James E. Talmage's *The Articles of Faith*, first published in 1899. Talmage later served as an apostle, and the book was influential for generations. It is still worth reading. But it is historical commentary: it shows how a learned Latter-day Saint explained the faith in his era. It does not settle what the Church teaches now. When you cite it, say so: "Talmage argued in 1899 that…" is accurate. "The Church teaches that…" would need a different source.

The working rule for commentary is simple. Name the author, name the date, and describe the claim as theirs until you find canonical or institutional support for it. Popularity does not change the category. A book can be quoted a million times and still be one author's interpretation.

## Historical records: what someone said, when

The fourth category is historical evidence: journals and diaries, meeting minutes, letters, newspaper reports, early printed sermons. Latter-day Saints have kept records from the beginning. Doctrine and Covenants 21:1 opens with the command that "there shall be a record kept among you." As a result, the historical record is unusually rich.

Historical sources answer historical questions. A diary entry from 1880 can show what its writer heard, or believed they heard, at a particular meeting. It can show that an idea was being discussed in a certain place and time. It cannot by itself show that the idea was the Church's doctrine then, and it says nothing at all about what the Church teaches today.

Records also need their own care. Was the writer present, or reporting what someone else said? Was the entry written that evening or years later? Do other sources from the same meeting agree? These are the same questions a historian asks of any document, and they apply with full force to religious history.

Historical records matter most when wording and emphasis change over time. The Church's guide says plainly that it does not rule out future additions or changes to its teachings or practices. A careful student does not hide such changes or treat them as scandals. They date each source and let the dates speak.

## Central and peripheral teachings

Not all teachings carry the same weight. The guide makes this point with a contrast. Some doctrines are more important than others and might be called core doctrines. The guide names the Atonement of Jesus Christ as an example. Others are peripheral. Its example is the location of the Garden of Eden, a subject on which members may hold varying views and which commentators sometimes wrongly treat as central.

The guide also recalls Joseph Smith's own summary. The testimony of the apostles and prophets concerning Christ's death, burial and resurrection is the foundation of the religion. All other things, he said, are only appendages to it.

This distinction protects you from two opposite errors. One is treating an obscure passage as if it defined the faith. The other is dismissing a central teaching because you have found an odd statement elsewhere. When you study a topic, ask where it sits. Is it named in the standard works and taught consistently in current Church publications? Or does it rest on a single passage, a single sermon, or a commentator's speculation?

Watch the vocabulary too. The guide notes that some Latter-day Saint terms carry meanings different from those in other traditions. Its example is being "born again," which Latter-day Saints tend to describe as a process rather than a single moment. Many disagreements turn out to be differences in definition. Defining your terms from the tradition's own sources is part of using a source well.

## The source ledger

The habits in this module come together in a simple tool you will use for the rest of the course: the source ledger. Every time you take a note on a teaching, record four things beside it.

**Claim.** What exactly does the source say? Quote it or paraphrase it closely, in the source's own terms.

**Source.** Which kind is it: canonical scripture, institutional teaching, commentary, or a historical record? Give the full reference, such as book, chapter and verse, or title, author and date.

**Setting.** Who said or wrote it, when, to whom, and for what purpose? A revelation addressed to one person, a conference address to the whole Church, and a private letter are different settings.

**Confidence.** How far does this source carry the claim you want to make? Write the limit down.

Here is a worked example. You want to write that Latter-day Saints expect further revelation.

Claim: "We believe that He will yet reveal many great and important things pertaining to the Kingdom of God."

Source: canonical scripture, Article of Faith 9, Pearl of Great Price.

Setting: one of thirteen statements of belief written by Joseph Smith in 1842, now part of the canon.

Confidence: high that the Church affirms an expectation of further revelation. It does not say what will be revealed, or when.

From that ledger entry you can write a sentence that is both strong and accurate: "Article of Faith 9 affirms that God will yet reveal 'many great and important things'; it does not specify what those will be." Compare that with "Mormons think the Church can change anything at any time." That sentence is broader than any source in this module supports.

Start your own ledger as you work through the readings. You will revise entries as you learn more, and in later courses you will be glad of the habit. The aim is not to hedge every sentence. It is to make every sentence say exactly as much as its source allows.

items.body:
# Making careful claims

## From source to sentence

In the last module you sorted sources into four kinds: canonical scripture, institutional teaching, commentary, and historical records. Sorting is the first half of careful study. The second half happens when you write. Every time you put a teaching into your own words, you make a claim, and a claim can say more or less than its source supports.

This module is about that second half. Its goal is simple to state and takes practice to do: every doctrinal claim you write should name its source and say where that source's support ends. A claim that does both is not timid. It is strong in exactly the way that matters, because anyone who checks it will find it true.

You will practice on one of the most important texts in Latter-day Saint scripture, Joseph Smith's account of his first vision, and on the fact that he described that experience more than once. Several accounts of one event are a natural test of careful claims. They reward the reader who notices which account says what, and they trip up the reader who blends them together.

## The four fields at work

The source ledger from module 1.1 has four fields: claim, source, setting and confidence. Here is how they work on a real passage.

Take Joseph Smith—History 1:17, where Joseph describes seeing "two Personages, whose brightness and glory defy all description." One of them, he writes, called him by name and said, pointing to the other, "This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!"

**Claim.** In this account, Joseph Smith says he saw two Personages, and that one introduced the other as his Beloved Son.

**Source.** Canonical scripture: Joseph Smith—History 1:17, in the Pearl of Great Price.

**Setting.** Joseph tells us the setting himself. Verse 1 says he wrote to answer "the many reports" circulating about the Church, and verse 2 dates the writing to 1838, "the eighth year since the organization" of the Church. The event itself, verse 14 says, happened "early in the spring of eighteen hundred and twenty."

**Confidence.** High that this is what the canonized account says. The ledger entry also tells you what kind of claim you can build on it: a claim about the account. To write about the event in general, as other accounts describe it, you would need those accounts too.

Notice how much the setting field adds. An account written in 1838 about an event in 1820, intended for a public that had heard hostile reports, is a particular kind of document. Knowing that does not make it less important. It tells you how to cite it precisely.

## Three common slips

Most overstatements fall into a few patterns. Learning to spot them in your own writing is more useful than memorizing rules.

**From one passage to everyone.** "This passage teaches X" becomes "Latter-day Saints believe X." The second sentence is a claim about millions of people, and a passage can't support it by itself. Institutional teaching can tell you what the Church teaches. Only evidence about members can tell you what members believe, and even then it rarely covers all of them.

**From one moment to always.** "This 1880 sermon says X" becomes "The Church teaches X." The first sentence is about a document with a date. The second is about the present. Module 1.1 showed why the gap matters: the Church's guide expects teachings and emphasis to develop, and a single statement on one occasion may be a personal view.

**From one speaker to the institution.** "Elder Y said X" becomes "Mormon doctrine says X." Who said something matters, but a speaker's title alone does not turn a statement into doctrine. The councils and sources named in the Church's guide do that work.

The repair for each slip is the same: put the source back into the sentence. "In the 1838 account…", "A current Church explanation says…", "One nineteenth-century sermon claimed…". Each of these is shorter than the hedge it replaces, and more informative.

## Reading a narrative carefully

Joseph Smith—History 1:1–20 is a story, and stories need their own kind of care. A narrative makes claims through events, speech and the narrator's comments, and these are not all the same kind of claim.

Some verses report circumstances. Verse 5 describes "an unusual excitement on the subject of religion" in the area around Manchester, beginning with the Methodists. Verses 7 and 8 describe Joseph's family and his own uncertainty: he leaned toward the Methodists but could not decide "who was right and who was wrong."

Some verses report Joseph's inner life. Verse 12 says no passage of scripture ever came "with more power to the heart of man" than James 1:5 did to his. That is a statement about his experience, and it is the kind of thing only the narrator can report.

Some verses report what was said to him. In verses 18 and 19 Joseph asks which church to join and is told to join none of them. The Personage, he writes, said "all their creeds were an abomination in his sight," and quoted words about drawing near "with their lips" while hearts are "far from me."

When you cite verse 19, the careful form names who is speaking in the account and what is being described: in Joseph Smith's 1838 account, the Personage condemns the creeds and their "professors" in answer to Joseph's question about which church to join. Two slips are common here. One drops the attribution and turns the verse into a general statement. The other stretches it into a claim the verse does not make, such as a claim about what Latter-day Saints today think of every individual Christian. For that, you would need other sources, and you would cite them.

The narrator's comments are a fourth kind of claim. Verse 20 closes with Joseph's own reflection that "the adversary was aware" early in his life that he would be "a disturber and an annoyer of his kingdom." That is Joseph's interpretation of his experience, offered as his.

## When there are several accounts

Joseph Smith described the First Vision more than once. The Church's page on First Vision accounts says he left four accounts of his own, and that five of his contemporaries also wrote accounts after hearing him describe it. He published two of his accounts; the best known is the one canonized in the Pearl of Great Price that you are reading in this module. The other two, his earliest written account from 1832 and a journal entry, were not published in his lifetime. The Church published them in the 1960s. All of the accounts were written more than a decade after the event.

The accounts agree in their center. The Church's page notes that they tell a consistent story and all emphasize Jesus Christ, who answers Joseph's questions. They also differ in ways a careful reader should notice.

- **Why he prayed.** The 1832 account says Joseph sought forgiveness of his sins. Later accounts emphasize his question about which church to join. The page describes these concerns as closely related in his mind.
- **Who appeared.** The 1832 account refers to "the Lord." Later accounts describe two Personages, God the Father and Jesus Christ, and one also mentions angels.
- **What was said.** The introduction "This is My Beloved Son" appears in the canonized account but not in the 1832 one.

The Church's page offers explanations of its own. People emphasize different parts of an experience for different audiences and purposes, and the accounts were written for different settings: a private history, a visitor, an official history and a newspaper editor's inquiry. Joseph's understanding of the vision's meaning also grew over time. The page adds that historians expect this kind of variation when an experience is retold from memory, and it compares the multiple New Testament accounts of Paul's conversion.

For a careful student the practical lesson is about wording. A claim about the First Vision should say which account it draws on whenever the accounts differ. "In the 1838 account, Joseph describes two Personages" is precise. "Joseph always said he saw two beings" is not, because the earliest account says something different. Where the accounts agree, you can say so: "Every account centers on Jesus Christ answering Joseph's prayer."

## Quoting in context

A quotation carries its context with it whether or not you include it. Leaving context out does not make a quote neutral. It quietly substitutes a new one.

Three habits keep quotations honest. First, quote enough to keep the meaning. If a verse begins with a condition, quote the condition. Second, say who is speaking within the text. A narrator, a character, a quoted prophet and a voice from heaven are different speakers, and scripture often contains all four. Third, keep the question the text was answering. Joseph's question in verse 18 was which church to join, and the answer in verse 19 answers that question.

The same habits apply in the other direction. If someone quotes a passage at you, ask what comes before and after it, who is speaking, and what question it answers. You will often find that the passage supports a narrower claim than the one built on it, and occasionally a broader one.

## Writing with the right confidence

Careful writing is not hedged writing. A sentence full of "perhaps" and "some might say" tells the reader nothing about where the evidence actually is. Precise verbs do that work better.

- **"States" or "says"** fits when the source says it in so many words. Article of Faith 9 states that God "will yet reveal many great and important things."
- **"Teaches"** fits when a source presents something as doctrine, especially canonical or institutional sources.
- **"Describes"** fits a narrative: Joseph Smith—History 1 describes a pillar of light.
- **"Suggests" or "implies"** marks your inference, and tells the reader to check your reasoning.
- **"Some members believe"** needs evidence about members, not about doctrine.

Here is a rewrite that puts the module together. The overbroad version: "Mormons believe God told Joseph Smith that all other churches are evil." The careful version: "In his 1838 account, canonized in Joseph Smith—History 1:19, Joseph Smith writes that he was told to join none of the churches of his day, and that the Personage called their creeds an abomination; earlier accounts describe the vision differently." The careful version is longer, but every word in it can be checked, and none of it claims more than the source shows.

items.body:
# The Godhead: three distinct beings

## Three named in one sentence

The first Article of Faith is a single sentence: "We believe in God, the Eternal Father, and in His Son, Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Ghost." Every Christian tradition names these three. What a tradition says about how they relate to one another is where the differences begin, and Latter-day Saint teaching has a distinctive answer.

Latter-day Saints use the word **Godhead** for the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost together. The Church's Gospel Topics page on the Godhead says they are three separate beings, with distinct roles, who are one in purpose and doctrine. This module works through the sources behind each part of that sentence: that they are distinct, what the canon says about their natures, what roles the Church assigns to each, and what "one" means in Latter-day Saint sources.

The next module compares this teaching with Nicene Christianity. For now, the aim is to describe the Latter-day Saint teaching accurately on its own terms, from its own sources, before setting it beside anything else.

## Distinct beings in the scriptures

Latter-day Saints point to scenes in which the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost appear or act at the same time, in different ways. Reading these scenes closely is the best way to see why the teaching takes the shape it does.

The baptism of Jesus in Matthew 3:13–17 is the classic example. Jesus comes up out of the water. The heavens open, and "the Spirit of God" descends "like a dove." A voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." In one scene, the Son stands in the river, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks.

Acts 7:55–56 records Stephen's vision just before his death. Full of the Holy Ghost, he "saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God." Joseph Smith—History 1:17, which you read in module 1.2, describes two Personages, one introducing the other: "This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!" In 3 Nephi 11, a voice from heaven announces "my Beloved Son" before the risen Christ descends to the people.

Latter-day Saint sources read these passages as showing three distinct beings. Other Christians read the same New Testament passages too, and they interpret them within their own teaching about God; you will see how in the next module. A careful claim here names the reading: "Latter-day Saints cite the baptism of Jesus, where the Son, the Spirit and the Father's voice appear together, as evidence that they are distinct beings."

## Bodies and spirit: Doctrine and Covenants 130

The most direct canonical statement about the natures of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost is Doctrine and Covenants 130:22: "The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's; the Son also; but the Holy Ghost has not a body of flesh and bones, but is a personage of Spirit." The verse then gives a reason: "Were it not so, the Holy Ghost could not dwell in us." Verse 23 adds that a person may receive the Holy Ghost, and the Holy Ghost may descend upon them "and not tarry."

Section 130 is not a single revelation in the way many sections are. It collects items of instruction Joseph Smith gave at Ramus, Illinois, in April 1843, on several subjects. That setting matters when you cite it. Verse 22 is canonical, and the Church's Godhead page cites it for exactly this teaching. Other verses in the section address different matters entirely, from the nature of angels to a prophecy about South Carolina. Cite the verse that supports your claim, not the section as a whole.

Read verse 22 for what it states and what it leaves open. It states that the Father and the Son each have a tangible body of flesh and bones, and that the Holy Ghost is a personage of Spirit. It does not say how this was so before Christ's mortal life, and it does not set out a full account of divine nature. When a reader moves from "the Father has a body" to detailed claims about what that body is like, they have left the verse behind. Mark that move as interpretation if you make it.

The same section opens with a related point. Verse 1 says that when the Savior appears, "we shall see that he is a man like ourselves," and verse 2 that the "same sociality" which exists here will exist there, "coupled with eternal glory." These verses help explain why embodiment matters in Latter-day Saint thought: the teaching about God is tied to a teaching about what human beings can become. That connection belongs to later courses, but it is worth noticing where it starts.

## Roles: Father, Son and Holy Ghost

The Church's Godhead page assigns each member a role. The Father is the ultimate object of worship; Latter-day Saints pray to him in the name of Jesus Christ. The Son is the Lord and Redeemer. The Holy Ghost is the messenger and revealer of the Father and the Son.

These roles show up in the scriptures you are reading. In John 17, Jesus prays to the Father. In 3 Nephi 11:11, the risen Christ says he has "glorified the Father in taking upon me the sins of the world." In 3 Nephi 11:32 he says the Holy Ghost "beareth record of the Father and me," which fits the description of the Holy Ghost as a witness and revealer.

Be careful not to turn roles into the whole picture. The page describes the three as perfectly united in carrying out the Father's plan; it does not say the Father has no part in redemption or the Son no part in revelation. Roles describe how the sources usually speak of each member. They are not a strict division of labor.

## What "one" means in Latter-day Saint sources

Scripture also speaks of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost as one. In 3 Nephi 11:27 Christ says "the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one," and 2 Nephi 31:21 ends Nephi's explanation of the doctrine of Christ with "the only and true doctrine of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, which is one God, without end."

Latter-day Saint sources explain this oneness as unity of purpose and doctrine among distinct beings. The Church's Godhead page says the three are perfectly united in carrying out the Father's plan of salvation. The passage Latter-day Saints most often cite for this reading is John 17. Praying for his disciples, Jesus asks "that they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." In verse 22 he prays "that they may be one, even as we are one."

The Latter-day Saint argument from John 17 runs like this: Jesus asks that his disciples be one in the same way that he and the Father are one, and the disciples remain distinct people, so the oneness in view must be a unity that distinct persons can share. You can state that argument accurately without endorsing it. You should also know that it is an argument about interpretation. Other Christian traditions read John 17 within their own understanding of God, and they do not draw the same conclusion.

Notice too that the word "God" can be used for the whole Godhead, as in 2 Nephi 31:21, or for the Father in particular, as in Article of Faith 1. When you quote a passage, check which use it makes.

## What the sources leave open

Part of describing a teaching accurately is knowing where its sources stop. The canonical and institutional sources in this module say a good deal: that the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost are distinct; that the Father and the Son have bodies of flesh and bones and the Holy Ghost is a personage of Spirit; what roles each fills; and that they are one in purpose.

They say much less about other questions people naturally ask. How exactly does the Holy Ghost "dwell in us"? What is the relationship of the Godhead to the Father's other creations? Popular writing sometimes fills these gaps with confident detail. A careful student labels such detail for what it is, commentary or speculation, and keeps it separate from what the sources teach.

This is not a weakness in the teaching. Every tradition's account of God includes acknowledged limits. Being clear about them is part of explaining any of them well.

## Explaining it well

Imagine a friend with no background asks you what Latter-day Saints believe about God. A good answer is short, uses the tradition's own words, cites its sources, and defines any word that might mislead. For example:

"Latter-day Saints believe in God the Father, his Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost, and call the three together the Godhead (Article of Faith 1). They teach that these are three distinct beings: in scripture the Church cites, like Jesus's baptism in Matthew 3, the Son, the Spirit and the Father's voice appear together. According to Doctrine and Covenants 130:22, the Father and the Son have bodies of flesh and bones, while the Holy Ghost is a personage of spirit. When scripture says they are 'one,' Latter-day Saints understand that as unity of purpose, not one being; the Church's Godhead page describes them as one in purpose and doctrine. 'Godhead' here means the three together, not a shared divine substance."

That paragraph is under 120 words. Every sentence attributes its claim, and the last sentence heads off a likely misunderstanding. It also avoids describing anyone else's belief, which is the subject of the next module.

# Unity language and the Nicene comparison

## Comparing fairly

Latter-day Saint teaching about the Godhead is often explained by contrast with the doctrine of the Trinity held by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant Christians. Contrast can be clarifying. It can also go badly wrong, because each tradition uses ordinary words like "one," "person" and "being" in specialized ways, and it is easy to describe the other side in terms it would never use for itself.

This module sets a standard for comparison that you will use throughout the course: describe each tradition so that its own members would recognize the description as fair. You will read a Book of Mormon chapter that speaks of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost as one, and the Catholic Church's own account of the Trinity in the Catechism of the Catholic Church. Then you will compare them carefully, noting where they really differ and where the differences are only apparent.

As always in this course, you are assessed on accuracy, not agreement. A Latter-day Saint who can explain the Trinity the way a Catholic theologian would, and a Catholic who can explain the Godhead the way a Latter-day Saint teacher would, have both learned something valuable.

## "One" in 3 Nephi 11

Third Nephi 11 describes the risen Jesus Christ appearing to people gathered at a temple in the land Bountiful. It is one of the Book of Mormon's central chapters, and it uses the language of oneness several times.

The chapter opens with a voice from heaven: "Behold my Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" (verse 7). Christ then descends and introduces himself (verse 10). Later, giving instructions for baptism, he says it should be done "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost" (verse 25), and adds: "the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one; and I am in the Father, and the Father in me, and the Father and I are one" (verse 27). Verse 36 repeats it: "the Father, and I, and the Holy Ghost are one."

The same chapter keeps the three distinct in how it speaks. The Father's voice introduces the Son. The Son says he has "suffered the will of the Father" (verse 11). The Holy Ghost bears record of the Father and the Son (verse 32). Latter-day Saint readers take the chapter's oneness language as unity of purpose and witness among distinct beings, consistent with what you studied in module 1.3. That is the tradition's reading of its own scripture, and you can describe it as such.

Notice also what the chapter says about disputes. Christ tells the people that "there shall be no disputations among you" about baptism or "the points of my doctrine" (verse 28), and that "the spirit of contention" is not of him (verse 29). That is a fitting text to keep in mind when comparing beliefs.

## The Trinity in its own words

The Catechism of the Catholic Church, the Catholic Church's official summary of its teaching, treats the Trinity in paragraphs 232 through 267. Several of its points are essential to describing the doctrine accurately.

The Trinity is called "the central mystery of Christian faith and life" (paragraph 234). The Catechism teaches that it is a mystery in a strict sense: something that could not be known unless God revealed it, and that human reason cannot fully grasp even after it is revealed (paragraph 237).

The Church confesses "one God in three persons" (paragraph 253). It does not confess three Gods. Each of the persons is fully God, and they do not divide the one divinity among themselves.

To say this precisely, the Catechism uses three technical terms (paragraph 252). **Substance**, also called essence or nature, names the divine being in its unity. **Person**, or hypostasis, names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in their real distinction from one another. **Relation** names the way that distinction consists in their relationships to one another: the Father begets, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds.

Finally, the persons are really distinct. They are not simply three ways the one God appears (paragraph 254). The Catechism also traces this teaching to the early councils: the Council of Nicaea in 325 confessed that the Son is "consubstantial" with the Father, and the Council of Constantinople in 381 confessed the Holy Spirit as "the Lord and giver of life" (paragraphs 242 and 245). The creed associated with these councils is usually called the Nicene Creed.

## Three caricatures to avoid

With those points in hand, you can recognize three common misdescriptions of the Trinity. Each one is rejected by the Catechism itself.

**"One God wearing three masks."** This view, that the Father, Son and Spirit are three modes or appearances of a single person, has a name: modalism. The Catechism rejects it when it says the persons are really distinct and not mere modes of the divine being (paragraph 254).

**"Three gods."** Some critics describe the Trinity as three gods with a single label. The Catechism explicitly says the Church does not confess three Gods but one God in three persons (paragraph 253).

**"The Son is a lesser, created being."** The councils the Catechism cites taught the opposite: the Son is consubstantial with the Father.

The same care runs both ways. Latter-day Saints are sometimes caricatured too, for example as not believing in Jesus Christ, when Article of Faith 1 and the scriptures in this module center on him. A fair comparison avoids both kinds of shortcut.

## Where the traditions really differ

Once the caricatures are cleared away, a real difference remains, and it is worth stating clearly.

Catholic teaching describes the Father, Son and Holy Spirit as three distinct persons who share one divine substance: one God. Latter-day Saint teaching describes the Father, Son and Holy Ghost as three distinct beings who are one in purpose. In Latter-day Saint sources, the Father and the Son each have a body of flesh and bones (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22).

So both traditions affirm that the three are distinct, and both affirm that they are one. The difference lies in what kind of oneness each affirms. For Catholic teaching, the oneness is a single divine substance. For Latter-day Saint teaching, it is unity of purpose among separate beings. That is a substantial difference, and neither side treats it as a misunderstanding of words. Stating it this way respects both.

## Same words, different meanings

Several words appear in both traditions with different meanings. A two-column glossary, as suggested in module 1.1, prevents most errors.

**One.** In the Catechism, the oneness of God is the unity of the divine substance. In Latter-day Saint sources, the oneness of the Godhead is unity of purpose and doctrine among distinct beings.

**Person.** In the Catechism, a technical term for the Father, Son and Spirit in their distinction, defined by relation. In Latter-day Saint usage, "personage" in scripture such as Doctrine and Covenants 130:22 refers to an individual being, embodied or a spirit.

**Being.** Latter-day Saint sources speak of three separate beings. Catholic teaching speaks of one divine being in three persons.

**God.** Both traditions use it of the Father in particular and of the divine as a whole. Check which use a source makes before you compare sentences.

When a sentence from one tradition is read with the other tradition's definitions, it can seem to say something absurd. That is a signal to go back to the glossary, not a discovery about the other side.

## Writing a fair comparison

A fair comparison follows a few steps.

1. Describe each tradition from its own authoritative sources: here, the Catechism for Catholic teaching and the standard works and Church publications for Latter-day Saint teaching.
2. Define the shared words separately for each tradition.
3. State what both affirm before stating where they differ.
4. Name the real difference in terms each side would accept.
5. Avoid saying what the other tradition "really" means beyond what its sources say.

Here is a short example. "Both Catholic and Latter-day Saint teaching name the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and affirm that they are both distinct and one. The Catechism teaches one God in three persons, distinct in their relations but sharing one divine substance. Latter-day Saint sources teach three separate beings, the Father and Son embodied, who are one in purpose. The Catechism rejects describing the Trinity as either three gods or one person in three roles."

Every claim in that paragraph can be checked against the readings in this module, and a member of either tradition could read it without feeling misrepresented.

items.body:
# The plan of salvation

## A plan with many names

Latter-day Saints often describe the whole of God's dealings with his children as a plan. The Book of Mormon gives it several names, sometimes in a single chapter. In Alma 42, a father teaching his son calls it "the great plan of salvation" (verse 5), "the great plan of happiness" (verse 8), "the plan of redemption" (verse 11) and "the plan of mercy" (verse 15). Each name highlights something different: rescue, joy, buying back what was lost, and mercy toward those who could not save themselves.

The Church's Gospel Topics page on the plan of salvation describes it as the plan that contains the laws and ordinances needed for eternal life. This module traces the plan's main parts through the canonical texts you will read and the Church's own summary. Later courses go deeper into each part. Here the goal is the overall shape, and the habit of keeping track of which source says what.

## God's stated purpose: Moses 1:39

The Book of Moses, in the Pearl of Great Price, records a vision in which Moses asks God why the creations exist and how they were made (Moses 1:30). The answer begins with a refusal to say everything: "For mine own purpose have I made these things. Here is wisdom and it remaineth in me" (verse 31). God then tells Moses that he created by his Only Begotten Son (verses 32–33), that there are "worlds without number" (verse 33), and that "only an account of this earth, and the inhabitants thereof" would be given (verse 35).

The vision ends with one of the most quoted verses in Latter-day Saint scripture: "For behold, this is my work and my glory—to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man" (verse 39).

Read the passage as a whole and two things stand out. First, it names a purpose: immortality and eternal life for human beings. Second, it is openly selective. Moses is told that God has created far more than he will learn about. A careful student keeps both points. Moses 1:39 is a strong source for the claim that, in Latter-day Saint scripture, God's work centers on human salvation. It is not a source for detailed claims about other worlds, which the passage deliberately declines to give.

## Before this life: Abraham 3

Latter-day Saint teaching holds that human beings lived before mortal birth. The Gospel Topics page puts it this way: before birth, people lived with heavenly parents as their spirit children. The canonical passage most often cited for the premortal council is Abraham 3:22–28.

In that passage, Abraham is shown "the intelligences that were organized before the world was," among them "many of the noble and great ones" (verse 22). God tells Abraham, "thou wast chosen before thou wast born" (verse 23). Then "one among them that was like unto God" proposes making an earth where these spirits may dwell, adding, "we will prove them herewith, to see if they will do all things whatsoever the Lord their God shall command them" (verses 24–25).

Verse 26 introduces two terms worth learning. Those "who keep their first estate shall be added upon," and those who "keep their second estate shall have glory added upon their heads for ever and ever." Latter-day Saint teaching generally reads the first estate as premortal life and the second as mortal life. The verse itself uses the terms without defining them, so when you explain them, attribute the explanation.

The passage ends with a choice. The Lord asks, "Whom shall I send?" One "like unto the Son of Man" answers, "Here am I, send me," and another answers the same. The Lord sends the first; the second "was angry, and kept not his first estate; and, at that day, many followed after him" (verses 27–28).

## The council and agency: Moses 4

Moses 4:1–4 tells the same council from another angle, and it adds the reason for the rejection. Satan proposed to "redeem all mankind, that one soul shall not be lost," and asked for God's honor (verse 1). The Beloved Son answered, "Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever" (verse 2). Satan, the passage says, "rebelled against me, and sought to destroy the agency of man" (verse 3), and was cast down.

Put the two passages side by side and notice what each contributes. Abraham 3 gives the setting and the purpose, proving the spirits, and the two volunteers. Moses 4 names the issue: agency. Neither passage says everything the other says. When you write about the council, cite the passage that supports each detail. The Gospel Topics page adds a detail of its own, that a third of Heavenly Father's spirit children followed Lucifer, and cites Revelation 12 for it. That detail comes from the page and the passage it cites, not from Abraham 3, which says only that "many followed after him."

Agency will be the subject of the next module. For now, notice how central it is: in Moses 4, the threat to the plan is not described as a threat to human happiness or to God's power, but to human choice.

## Mortal life: bodies, choices and trials

The Gospel Topics page lists several purposes of mortal life. Gaining a physical body is one of them. Agency is another: the page describes choice as essential to the plan, including the choice to repent and to receive ordinances such as baptism and confirmation. The page also says that earth life brings both joy and adversity, including temptation, opposition and trials, and that these can help people become more like their Heavenly Father.

Abraham 3:25 frames mortality as a test: "we will prove them herewith." Alma 42:4 calls it "a probationary time, a time to repent and serve God," and verse 10 "a preparatory state." These descriptions fit together. Mortality, in this teaching, is neither an accident nor a punishment. It is a stage with a purpose.

## Christ's Atonement at the center

Every name for the plan in Alma 42 points to the same center. "The plan of mercy could not be brought about except an atonement should be made," Alma says, and "therefore God himself atoneth for the sins of the world" (verse 15). The Gospel Topics page says that Jesus Christ overcame both physical and spiritual death, and that his Atonement was necessary because no unclean thing can dwell with God.

Alma 42 is also careful about how mercy works. Mercy does not cancel justice: "What, do ye suppose that mercy can rob justice? I say unto you, Nay; not one whit" (verse 25). Instead, "mercy claimeth the penitent, and mercy cometh because of the atonement" (verse 23). This is an important point for accurate description. In this teaching, the Atonement is how justice and mercy are both satisfied, not a suspension of justice.

## After this life

The Gospel Topics page summarizes what follows death. At death the spirit separates from the body and continues to live. Those who have lived righteously enter a state the page calls spirit paradise, citing Alma's description of "a state of rest, a state of peace." Because of Christ's Atonement, all people will be resurrected, their spirits and bodies reunited. A final judgment follows, in which, according to the page, people are judged according to their desires and their obedience to the commandments.

Alma 42:23 compresses much of this into one sentence: "the atonement bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead; and the resurrection of the dead bringeth back men into the presence of God; and thus they are restored into his presence, to be judged according to their works."

Later courses cover the spirit world, resurrection and judgment in depth, including the degrees of glory described in Doctrine and Covenants 76. For this module, the outline is enough: premortal life, the council, mortal life, the Atonement, death, resurrection and judgment.

## Keeping the outline honest

The plan of salvation is often taught with a diagram: circles and arrows from premortal life to the kingdoms of glory. Diagrams are useful. They also make every part look equally certain and equally detailed, which the sources are not.

As you build your own outline, keep the source ledger habit. For each stage, write the passage or page that teaches it. Mark where the canon is explicit, where the Church's summary adds detail, and where an explanation is interpretation. "Abraham 3:26 says those who keep their second estate will have glory added upon their heads" is a quotation. "The second estate is mortal life" is a widely taught reading of it. Both belong in your notes, labeled differently.

Above all, notice what the sources themselves put at the center. Alma's names for the plan, Moses 1:39's statement of purpose, and the Church's summary all point to the same place: the Atonement of Jesus Christ and the eternal life of God's children.

items.title: Agency and the Fall
items.body:
# Agency and the Fall

## Why agency comes first

In module 2.1 you read that Satan "sought to destroy the agency of man" (Moses 4:3). In Latter-day Saint scripture, the conflict at the heart of the premortal council was not about whether people would be saved but about whether they would choose. This module asks why agency matters so much in Latter-day Saint teaching, and how it connects to one of the most distinctive Latter-day Saint teachings of all: that the Fall of Adam and Eve was a necessary step in God's plan, not simply a catastrophe.

Your main text is 2 Nephi 2, a father's blessing to his son. Lehi, near the end of his life, speaks to his son Jacob about redemption, opposition, choice and the Fall. It is one of the densest theological chapters in the Book of Mormon, and it rewards slow reading. You will also read Moses 4:1–4 and 5:9–12, which give the premortal setting of agency and Adam and Eve's own response to their fall.

## Opposition in all things

The heart of Lehi's argument is a claim about the structure of the world: "it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things" (2 Nephi 2:11). Without opposition, he says, "righteousness could not be brought to pass, neither wickedness, neither holiness nor misery, neither good nor bad."

Lehi then builds a chain of reasoning in verse 13. If there is no law, there is no sin; if no sin, no righteousness; if no righteousness, no happiness; and so on, until "if these things are not there is no God." The argument runs from the existence of moral alternatives to the meaning of the whole creation. Its point is that good and evil, happiness and misery, are only meaningful in a world where both are possible.

When you summarize this, keep it attributed and keep it tied to its purpose. Lehi is not giving a general theory of physics. He is explaining why a world with real moral choice, and therefore real possibility of sin, is necessary to God's "eternal purposes."

## To act and not to be acted upon

From opposition, Lehi moves to agency. God created "things to act and things to be acted upon" (verse 14). He set "the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life" (verse 15), and "gave unto man that he should act for himself" (verse 16). Then comes a striking qualification: "man could not act for himself save it should be that he was enticed by the one or the other."

Later in the chapter Lehi says that because people are redeemed from the Fall, they have "become free forever, knowing good from evil; to act for themselves and not to be acted upon" (verse 26). They are "free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death" (verse 27).

Two things are worth noticing. First, agency in this chapter requires real alternatives and real enticement in both directions. Second, the freedom Lehi describes is connected to Christ: it is through redemption from the Fall that people become free to choose. Agency in this teaching is not simply a natural fact. It is a gift that depends on the Redeemer.

## Agency in the premortal council

Moses 4:1–4, which you read in module 2.1, frames agency as the issue in the premortal council. Satan offered to redeem everyone, "that one soul shall not be lost," in exchange for God's honor (verse 1). The Beloved Son said, "Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever" (verse 2). Satan "sought to destroy the agency of man" and was cast down (verse 3), becoming "the father of all lies, to deceive and to blind men, and to lead them captive at his will" (verse 4).

Read with 2 Nephi 2, the logic is consistent. A plan that guaranteed no one would be lost would have removed real choice. In Lehi's terms, it would have removed the opposition that makes righteousness and happiness possible. Lehi's description of the devil fits too: he "sought also the misery of all mankind" (2 Nephi 2:18), "that all men might be miserable like unto himself" (verse 27).

## The Fall as a step forward

The most distinctive part of 2 Nephi 2 is its account of the Fall. Lehi says that if Adam had not transgressed, he and Eve "would have remained in the garden of Eden," and all things "must have remained in the same state" (verse 22). "They would have had no children; wherefore they would have remained in a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery; doing no good, for they knew no sin" (verse 23).

Then come two famous sentences: "all things have been done in the wisdom of him who knoweth all things" (verse 24), and "Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy" (verse 25).

Moses 5 gives Adam and Eve's own reaction. After the Holy Ghost bore witness to Adam that "as thou hast fallen thou mayest be redeemed" (verse 9), Adam rejoiced: "because of my transgression my eyes are opened, and in this life I shall have joy, and again in the flesh I shall see God" (verse 10). Eve said, "Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed, and never should have known good and evil, and the joy of our redemption, and the eternal life which God giveth unto all the obedient" (verse 11).

The picture these passages give is consistent. The Fall brought mortality, children, knowledge of good and evil, and the need for redemption, and Adam and Eve themselves are portrayed as glad of it once they understand the plan. Notice the vocabulary: these passages speak of Adam's "transgression," and Lehi says Adam "fell." Latter-day Saint teaching often uses "transgression" for the Fall, and you should quote the passages' own words when you describe it.

## Responsibility: Article of Faith 2

If the Fall was part of the plan, are people responsible for it? Article of Faith 2 answers directly: "men will be punished for their own sins, and not for Adam's transgression."

Read that sentence for exactly what it says. It denies that anyone is punished for Adam's transgression. It affirms that people are accountable for their own sins. It does not say that the Fall had no effects. 2 Nephi 2 and Alma 42 describe real effects: mortality, separation from God's presence, and a fallen condition from which people must be redeemed (Alma 42:6–9). The article distinguishes consequences of the Fall from guilt for it.

This is a point where Latter-day Saint teaching is often compared with traditions that teach some form of original sin. A fair comparison requires reading those traditions in their own sources, which this course does in a later module. For now, describe the Latter-day Saint teaching accurately: people are not punished for Adam's transgression, and they are accountable for their own sins.

## Redemption from the Fall

Lehi's chapter is not mainly about the Fall. It is about the Redeemer. "Redemption cometh in and through the Holy Messiah; for he is full of grace and truth," Lehi says (verse 6). "He offereth himself a sacrifice for sin, to answer the ends of the law, unto all those who have a broken heart and a contrite spirit" (verse 7). No one, he says, can "dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah" (verse 8).

And again, near the end: "the Messiah cometh in the fulness of time, that he may redeem the children of men from the fall" (verse 26). The Fall and the Atonement belong together in this teaching. To describe the Fall without the redemption it was meant to be answered by is to describe half the doctrine.

## Describing it well

A good short explanation of this module's teaching keeps three things together: agency, the Fall and redemption. For example:

"In 2 Nephi 2, Lehi teaches that God gave people the power to 'act for themselves,' which requires real alternatives, or 'opposition in all things.' Latter-day Saint scripture describes the Fall as a necessary step: without it, Adam and Eve 'would have had no children' (2 Nephi 2:23), and 'Adam fell that men might be' (verse 25). Article of Faith 2 adds that people are punished for their own sins, not for Adam's transgression. The same chapter centers on Christ, who redeems people from the Fall so they can choose eternal life."

Each claim there is attributed and bounded. It describes the teaching without claiming to describe every member's view, and without describing other traditions it hasn't read.

items.title: Faith, repentance and baptism
items.body:
# Faith, repentance and baptism

## The doctrine of Christ

The Book of Mormon uses a specific phrase for the way a person comes to Christ: "the doctrine of Christ." Nephi uses it in 2 Nephi 31 and 32, and the risen Christ uses it in 3 Nephi 11, where he says, "this is my doctrine" and describes repentance, belief and baptism (3 Nephi 11:31–39). In these chapters the phrase does not mean all of Christian teaching. It names a particular pattern: faith in Christ, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost, and enduring to the end.

Article of Faith 4, which you read in module 1.1, gives the first part of that pattern in compact form: "the first principles and ordinances of the Gospel are: first, Faith in the Lord Jesus Christ; second, Repentance; third, Baptism by immersion for the remission of sins; fourth, Laying on of hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost."

This module studies the first steps, faith, repentance and baptism, mainly through 2 Nephi 31. The next module takes up the Holy Ghost and enduring. Together they cover the pattern Latter-day Saints call the doctrine of Christ.

## Christ's own baptism

Nephi begins with a question. If Jesus, "being holy," needed to be baptized "to fulfil all righteousness," how much more do "we, being unholy" (2 Nephi 31:5)? The phrase "fulfil all righteousness" comes from Matthew 3:15, where Jesus answers John's hesitation to baptize him.

Nephi then explains what Christ's baptism showed. Jesus "humbleth himself before the Father, and witnesseth unto the Father that he would be obedient unto him in keeping his commandments" (verse 7). After he was baptized, "the Holy Ghost descended upon him in the form of a dove" (verse 8). And it showed "the straitness of the path, and the narrowness of the gate" (verse 9). Christ, in this reading, was baptized not because he needed forgiveness but as an act of obedience and an example to follow.

Verse 10 draws the conclusion in Christ's own words: "Follow thou me." Nephi adds, "can we follow Jesus save we shall be willing to keep the commandments of the Father?"

## Faith and repentance

In this pattern, faith in Jesus Christ comes first, and it is not passive. Nephi describes it as following the Son "with full purpose of heart, acting no hypocrisy and no deception before God, but with real intent" (verse 13). Later he says that people enter the path "by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save" (verse 19).

Repentance is joined to faith throughout the chapter. The Father's voice says, "Repent ye, repent ye, and be baptized in the name of my Beloved Son" (verse 11). In 3 Nephi 11:32, Christ says the Father "commandeth all men, everywhere, to repent and believe in me."

These passages present repentance as turning toward God, made possible by Christ, and expressed in action. Alma 36, which you will read in the next module, gives a vivid narrative of one person's repentance. For now, note how the doctrinal passages connect it to faith and baptism rather than treating it as a separate topic.

## Baptism: the gate

Nephi's image for baptism is a gate. "The gate by which ye should enter is repentance and baptism by water; and then cometh a remission of your sins by fire and by the Holy Ghost" (verse 17). After entering, a person is "in this strait and narrow path which leads to eternal life" (verse 18).

The image does two things. It marks baptism as a beginning, not an end; a gate opens onto a path. And it places baptism and the Holy Ghost together: water baptism is followed by "the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost" (verse 13). In Latter-day Saint practice, the gift of the Holy Ghost is conferred by the laying on of hands after baptism, as Article of Faith 4 states.

The New Testament gives a parallel pattern. On the day of Pentecost, Peter told his hearers, "Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost" (Acts 2:38). Latter-day Saints cite this passage alongside 2 Nephi 31 as evidence that the pattern is the same in both books.

## How baptism is performed

Two Book of Mormon passages describe the manner of baptism. In 3 Nephi 11:23–26, Christ gives the words to be spoken, "Having authority given me of Jesus Christ, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen," and then says, "shall ye immerse them in the water, and come forth again out of the water." Article of Faith 4 specifies "baptism by immersion."

The same passage ties baptism to authority. Christ gives Nephi and others "power" to baptize (verses 21–22), and the prescribed words begin, "Having authority given me of Jesus Christ." Article of Faith 5 states the general principle: a person must be "called of God, by prophecy, and by the laying on of hands by those who are in authority," to administer the ordinances of the gospel. In Latter-day Saint teaching, authority is part of what makes a baptism valid. That is one reason the Church baptizes converts even if they were baptized in another tradition.

## The baptismal covenant

Latter-day Saint teaching describes baptism as entering a covenant, a two-way promise with God. The clearest scriptural description is in Mosiah 18, where Alma invites people at the waters of Mormon to be baptized.

Alma describes those who are ready as "desirous to come into the fold of God, and to be called his people," and "willing to bear one another's burdens, that they may be light; yea, and are willing to mourn with those that mourn; yea, and comfort those that stand in need of comfort, and to stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places" (verses 8–9). Baptism, he says, is "a witness before him that ye have entered into a covenant with him, that ye will serve him and keep his commandments, that he may pour out his Spirit more abundantly upon you" (verse 10).

Notice the structure. The people promise to serve God, keep his commandments and care for one another. God's promise is to pour out his Spirit. When you describe the baptismal covenant, cite Mosiah 18:8–10 for these specific terms, and 2 Nephi 31:13 for the promise to take upon oneself the name of Christ.

## A sequence, not a checklist

It is easy to turn the doctrine of Christ into a checklist: faith, done; repentance, done; baptism, done. Nephi resists that reading directly. After the gate, he asks, "I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay" (verse 19). The next module takes up what follows.

For now, notice how Nephi ends the chapter: "this is the way; and there is none other way nor name given under heaven whereby man can be saved in the kingdom of God. And now, behold, this is the doctrine of Christ, and the only and true doctrine of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, which is one God, without end" (verse 21). The pattern is presented as a way of life centered on Christ, not a set of tasks.

## Describing it well

A careful short explanation might read: "Latter-day Saints call the pattern in 2 Nephi 31 'the doctrine of Christ': faith in Jesus Christ, repentance, baptism by immersion, and the gift of the Holy Ghost, followed by enduring to the end. Nephi calls repentance and baptism 'the gate' to a path leading to eternal life (verses 17–18). In Mosiah 18:8–10, baptism is a covenant to serve God, keep his commandments and care for others, with God's promise of his Spirit. Article of Faith 5 adds that the ordinance requires authority from God."

That explanation names its passages, uses their own terms, and describes the practice without claiming more than the sources state.

items.title: The Holy Ghost and enduring to the end
items.body:
# The Holy Ghost and enduring to the end

## After the gate

At the end of 2 Nephi 31, after describing faith, repentance and baptism, Nephi asks whether "all is done" and answers, "Nay" (verse 19). This module takes up what comes next in the doctrine of Christ: the gift of the Holy Ghost, the guidance it is said to give, and enduring to the end.

These subjects involve claims about spiritual experience: that the Holy Ghost teaches, witnesses and guides. As throughout this course, your task is to describe those claims accurately from their sources. You will not be asked about your own experience, and nothing in this module assesses belief. A careful description of what Latter-day Saint scripture says about the Holy Ghost is a skill like any other.

## Who the Holy Ghost is

You met the Holy Ghost's nature in module 1.3. Doctrine and Covenants 130:22 says the Holy Ghost "has not a body of flesh and bones, but is a personage of Spirit," and adds, "Were it not so, the Holy Ghost could not dwell in us." The Church's Godhead page describes the Holy Ghost as the messenger and revealer of the Father and the Son.

Several passages describe the Holy Ghost's work as witness. In 3 Nephi 11:32, Christ says that "the Holy Ghost beareth record of the Father and me." In 2 Nephi 31:18, the Holy Ghost "witnesses of the Father and the Son." Jesus tells his disciples in John 14:26 that "the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you."

Keep these roles distinct when you write about them: witnessing of the Father and Son, teaching, and bringing to remembrance. Each passage supports a particular description.

## The gift of the Holy Ghost

Latter-day Saint teaching distinguishes the influence of the Holy Ghost, which anyone may feel, from the gift of the Holy Ghost, given after baptism by the laying on of hands (Article of Faith 4). The scriptures you have read reflect this sequence. In 2 Nephi 31:12, the voice of the Son says, "He that is baptized in my name, to him will the Father give the Holy Ghost, like unto me." Acts 2:38 promises "the gift of the Holy Ghost" to those who repent and are baptized.

Doctrine and Covenants 130:23 adds a caution: "A man may receive the Holy Ghost, and it may descend upon him and not tarry with him." The gift, in this teaching, is a continuing relationship that can be lost, not a single event.

## "Feast upon the words of Christ"

In 2 Nephi 32, Nephi answers a question he senses his readers are asking: what should they do after entering the path? His first answer is about the words of Christ. "Angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost; wherefore, they speak the words of Christ. Wherefore, I said unto you, feast upon the words of Christ; for behold, the words of Christ will tell you all things what ye should do" (verse 3).

His second answer is about the Holy Ghost: "if ye will enter in by the way, and receive the Holy Ghost, it will show unto you all things what ye should do" (verse 5). The two answers belong together. In Nephi's teaching, the words of Christ and the Holy Ghost both guide those on the path.

Then Nephi turns to prayer. "The evil spirit teacheth not a man to pray, but teacheth him that he must not pray" (verse 8). "Ye must pray always, and not faint; ... ye shall pray unto the Father in the name of Christ, that he will consecrate thy performance unto thee, that thy performance may be for the welfare of thy soul" (verse 9). Notice again the pattern of prayer from module 1.3: to the Father, in the name of Christ.

## Moroni's promise

Near the very end of the Book of Mormon, Moroni addresses future readers. He asks them to "remember how merciful the Lord hath been" and "ponder it in your hearts" (Moroni 10:3). Then he makes a promise: "ask God, the Eternal Father, in the name of Christ, if these things are not true; and if ye shall ask with a sincere heart, with real intent, having faith in Christ, he will manifest the truth of it unto you, by the power of the Holy Ghost" (verse 4). And: "by the power of the Holy Ghost ye may know the truth of all things" (verse 5).

Read the promise for its conditions. It asks for remembering, pondering and asking; it specifies asking the Father in Christ's name; and it names sincerity, real intent and faith in Christ. Latter-day Saint teaching often refers to this passage simply as "Moroni's promise." When you describe it, quote its conditions as well as its promise. A summary that leaves the conditions out misdescribes the passage.

Moroni 7 gives a related principle for discernment that Latter-day Saints often cite: "every thing which inviteth to do good, and to persuade to believe in Christ, is sent forth by the power and gift of Christ" (Moroni 7:16). That passage is about the Spirit of Christ given to every person, and you can note it as a related source rather than a description of the gift of the Holy Ghost.

## Repentance and joy: Alma 36

Alma 36 is a father's account of his own conversion. Alma the Younger tells his son Helaman that he once fought against the Church, and describes three days and nights of torment as he remembered his sins (verses 12–16). Then he remembered his father's teaching "concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world" (verse 17), and cried out in his heart, "O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me" (verse 18).

What follows is one of the most vivid passages in the Book of Mormon: "I could remember my pains no more" (verse 19); "what joy, and what marvelous light I did behold" (verse 20); "there can be nothing so exquisite and sweet as was my joy" (verse 21). From then on, Alma says, he "labored without ceasing" to bring others to "taste of the exceeding joy" he had tasted, that they "might also be born of God, and be filled with the Holy Ghost" (verse 24).

Alma 36 is a narrative of personal experience, and it should be described as one: Alma's account, told to his son, of his own repentance. It is also a text Latter-day Saints use to teach what repentance through Christ can mean. Both statements are accurate; keep them distinct.

## Enduring to the end

The final step of the doctrine of Christ is to endure. In 2 Nephi 31:15 the Father's voice says, "He that endureth to the end, the same shall be saved," and Nephi concludes that "unless a man shall endure to the end, in following the example of the Son of the living God, he cannot be saved" (verse 16).

Nephi then describes what enduring looks like, and it is not grim persistence. "Ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life" (verse 20).

Read closely, enduring in this verse has content: steadfastness in Christ, hope, love of God and others, and feasting on the word. It is the same pattern as the rest of the doctrine of Christ, continued through life.

## Describing it well

A careful short explanation might read: "In the Latter-day Saint pattern Nephi calls the doctrine of Christ, baptism is followed by the gift of the Holy Ghost (2 Nephi 31:12–13; Article of Faith 4), which Nephi says 'will show unto you all things what ye should do' (2 Nephi 32:5). Nephi teaches that those on the path must 'feast upon the words of Christ,' pray to the Father in Christ's name, and 'endure to the end' by pressing forward with hope and love (2 Nephi 31:20). Moroni 10:4–5 promises that those who ask God sincerely, with real intent and faith in Christ, can know truth by the power of the Holy Ghost."

The explanation describes what the texts promise and teach. It does not tell the reader what to believe or claim anything about any particular person's experience.

items.title: Premortal life, creation, and the Fall
items.body: Creation narratives teach through structure, imagery, and theological emphasis. Read each account in its own setting before combining it with another. A passage about divine purpose does not automatically establish a mechanism, scientific date, or complete physical history. Latter-day Saint accounts connect creation and the Fall with agency, mortality, and redemption. That connection should not erase the narrative’s difficulty or make every consequence of mortality desirable. Distinguish what the text affirms, what an institutional explanation adds, and what a modern reader supplies. Comparison is especially useful when one account emphasizes order and another emphasizes relationship or choice. Your task is to explain those emphases with textual evidence, while leaving scientific and historical claims at the level their evidence supports.

items.title: Atonement, grace, and transformation
items.body: An account of grace becomes distorted when divine help is treated as a prize for already being good enough. Read texts about mercy and reconciliation before constructing an effort-versus-grace formula. Latter-day Saint teaching includes both dependence on Christ and invitations to act; understanding their relationship requires attention to the passage’s purpose. A response to grace is not necessarily a competing source of salvation. Also distinguish forgiveness, resurrection, healing, and sanctification rather than using “Atonement” as an unexplained answer to every question. A fictional pastoral example can reveal a hidden assumption: what would you say to someone who believes one failure makes divine help unavailable? Support your answer with a passage, and avoid claiming to determine that person’s standing before God.

items.title: Revelation, discernment, and stewardship
items.body: Revelation is a theological claim about divine communication, and discernment concerns how people interpret what they believe they have received. A feeling should not become an automatic warrant to control someone else. Study the connection between inquiry, preparation, and reflection, while recognizing that a course cannot verify the divine origin of an individual experience. Stewardship helps define the limits of a claim: guidance for one’s own responsibilities differs from a binding instruction for a community. When sources appear to conflict, slow down. Identify the exact claim, consult appropriate sources, consider alternative explanations, and avoid rushing into consequential action. Learning how a tradition understands revelation is compatible with uncertainty and with respecting a learner who interprets spiritual experience differently.

items.title: Priesthood, keys, authority, and service
items.body: Related terms should not be treated as synonyms. Priesthood discussions may concern divine power, authorization to act, an office, or the right to direct particular work. Ask which meaning is operating in each sentence. An explanation of keys is incomplete if it never explains whose responsibilities they govern. A discussion of power is incomplete if it suggests that position alone proves righteousness. Study descriptions of persuasion, patience, and love alongside accounts of organization. Current institutional guidance helps prevent a learner from making administrative claims from memory. A useful diagram connects responsibilities and service while avoiding a ladder of human worth. When discussing women and men, distinguish the Church’s current descriptions from historical practices and from a scholar’s interpretation.

items.title: Resurrection, judgment, and eternal life
items.body: Questions about the afterlife invite more certainty than sources sometimes supply. Begin by separating resurrection, judgment, salvation, and exaltation. A text may speak broadly about life after death while another describes differentiated outcomes. Treat each in context before creating a chart. Hope does not remove responsibility, and responsibility does not authorize a learner to pronounce another person’s eternal destination. Particular symbols and descriptions may resist a literal diagram. Mark what is explicit, what is interpreted, and what remains unknown. This method makes room for the tradition’s distinctive teachings while preventing confident speculation about individual cases, detailed geography of heaven, or the timing of every event.

items.title: Zion, consecration, and practical ethics
items.body: Doctrine becomes ethically thin when it never changes how a community treats people. Texts about Zion and consecration invite attention to shared life, material need, and responsibility. They do not automatically settle every contemporary policy dispute. Begin with the passage’s moral claims, then identify the additional evidence needed for a practical proposal. A service plan should describe whose needs it addresses, how their preferences will be heard, and how harm or paternalism will be avoided. Distinguish charity from using another person as an opportunity to display one’s virtue. Course progress can demonstrate an ability to reason about these responsibilities; it should not depend on disclosing donations, income, or private acts of service.

The learning goal is to make defensible distinctions and notice ambiguity, not to force every example into a perfectly tidy category.
